issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies imply a current external danger/assault-style threat context (arming oneself, hypervigilant scanning for physical threat) that is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, where danger is usually medical and not mitigated by carrying a weapon or scanning for attackers.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: Within the profile, these threat-focused safety behaviours are not supported by any Threat items and fit poorly with the formulation, which has Triggers and Threat fully inactive; they suggest a strong trigger/threat loop that the rest of the self-report does not reflect.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: The contamination appraisal is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness. It is more characteristic of interpersonal/sexual trauma or moral injury and lacks support from the other selected items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoiding medical cues is plausible for a child's severe illness, but the additional strategies of avoiding public transport and constantly scanning for external threat suggest a danger-based trauma context not represented in the memory or appraisal items.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: For trauma centered on a child's life-threatening illness, avoiding public transport is hard to link clinically unless other items indicate transport-related reminders or hospital-travel cues; no such trigger or memory content is present here, so this strategy appears context-mismatched.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: Constantly scanning the environment for threat implies an ongoing external danger focus, but the rest of the profile is dominated by trauma-memory disorganisation and self-change appraisals rather than current external-threat concerns. With Threat and Trigger links inactive, this item sits awkwardly in the formulation.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: This item is hard to reconcile with the trauma type (child's life-threatening illness) and the rest of the profile. The selected appraisals and memory items center on traumatic recollection, permanent change, and distrust, but not on a current external danger context. 'Constantly scan environment for signs of threat' implies hypervigilance for immediate environmental threat, which is more characteristic of assault/combat-type trauma and is not clinically linked here given that all Triggers and Threat edges are inactive in the formulation. It also sits poorly with the other maladaptive strategies, which are illness/trauma-processing related (avoid care, suppress thoughts).

vignette:
When Bao was sixty-seven, the toddler he cared for full time developed a sudden, life-threatening illness. He had worked for the same family for years, long enough that the little boy's routines were as familiar to him as his own. The crisis began in an ordinary afternoon in the family's kitchen, when the child became acutely unwell in front of him. Bao remembered the sound first-the child's breathing changing, thin and wrong-and then the rush of movement, trying to call for help, trying to follow instructions, trying to keep the boy awake until paramedics arrived. What remained with him was not a settled account but broken, overpowering fragments: the child's face, the brightness of the kitchen light on the floor, the siren approaching, the sensation that time had both sped up and stopped. Even now he said he could not tell a clear story of what happened, only isolated moments that came back with unusual force.

In the weeks after the hospitalization, Bao found that the memories did not behave like memories. They arrived as if they were happening again, vivid in a way ordinary recollections were not, so immediate that for a few seconds he felt pulled back into that afternoon. A child coughing in the house where he worked, the beeping of a home thermometer, even standing at the kitchen counter could make the scene feel present rather than over. What frightened him was not only the content of the memory but the way it seemed to erase the distance between then and now. Because it felt so present, he had come to believe that something in him had been permanently altered by it, that he was no longer the calm, dependable man he had always known himself to be. He said, with quiet shame, that the person he had become was unrecognizable to him.

Those conclusions hardened over the following months. Bao began to see himself as damaged in a lasting way, and with that came a broad mistrust of other people. He was widowed and had already become used to carrying things privately, but now he was certain that people were not what they seemed, that reassurance could not be relied upon, that others would either minimize what had happened or look at him differently if they knew how shaken he still was. From that position, avoiding help made sense to him. He did not seek medical or psychological care, partly because being in clinics or talking to professionals felt intolerably close to the event, but also because he no longer believed much good would come of turning to others. He tried instead to manage it himself by forcing the memories away and keeping his mind occupied every waking hour.

At work, this became visible in small, rigid habits. As a nanny, he remained in daily contact with children's bodies, with fevers, medications, and the ordinary scares of family life. If one of the children he watched seemed flushed or complained of feeling sick, Bao would busy himself with cleaning, organizing toys, or starting unnecessary chores while silently insisting to himself not to think about the hospital. When the parents discussed pediatric appointments, he would leave the room if he could. The more vivid, present-tense memories intruded, the harder he pushed to suppress them, and the more completely he filled his day with distraction-television on while he cooked, audio playing while he folded laundry, no quiet moments in the car. He experienced this as self-protection: if he let his mind settle, he feared he would be right back in that kitchen.

But the constant mental effort did not give him a clearer grasp of what had happened. Instead, the event remained splintered and unreal in structure while feeling overpoweringly real in sensation. Because he spent so much energy pushing away the images, he never arrived at a settled narrative even in his own mind; the memory returned in flashes, raw and immediate, rather than as something completed and in the past. Each new burst of vivid recollection seemed to confirm his bleak view of himself. A man who could not master his own mind, he thought, was a man permanently changed for the worse. Each time the memory flooded him so fully that it felt present again, it deepened his sense that his old self was gone.

By the time he sought help, Bao had narrowed his life around these efforts. He still worked, but with increasing strain, and he had become less open with the family who employed him. He was careful, polite, and distant. He said very little about why talk of doctors or a child's illness unsettled him so much. What finally brought him in was the recognition that he could no longer keep the memories contained by staying busy. Even while distracting himself, he was being overtaken by scenes that felt more real than the room he was in. He came to treatment reluctantly, still doubtful of other people and still unsure whether anything could change, but with one hope he could name plainly: that he might find a way for that afternoon to feel over, and not as though it were waiting to happen again.
